newsitem.title: ITALY: Profits rise 12 percent at Italy's Stet.
newsitem.headline: Profits rise 12 percent at Italy's Stet.

text.p: Stet, the state-owned telecommunications company due to be sold by the government early next year, said pretax profits climbed 12 percent in the first half of 1996 and promised a substantial improvement in full year results.

Stet, which holds majority stakes in telephone operator Telecom Italia and cellular phone firm Telecom Italia Mobile, said pretax profit in the first six months of the year rose to 4.04 trillion lire ($2.67 billion).
Sales at the company, which is itself controlled by giant state holding company IRI, climbed 9 percent over the same period to 19.64 trillion lire ($12.98 billion).
Expectations of a 7 percent rise in sales for the full year "leads us to see an economic performance for this year which will be significantly better than in 1995," the company said in a statement.
The group, which is headed by Ernesto Pascale, said it was undertaking a large investment programme to prepare the company for the full deregulation of the telecommunications market in the year 2000.

It said investments in the first half rose 31 percent to 4.6 trillion lire ($3.04 billion) from the comparable 1995 period. Between 1997 and 1999, it intended to plunge another 35.5 trillion lire ($23.46 billion) into investments, it said.

The investments will be self-financed allowing the group to cut its debt, Stet said. Much of the investment will go towards upgrading technology at Telecom Italia and TIM, but some of it has been earmarked for international expansion.

Stet has focused much of its foreign expansion efforts in Latin America and Europe as well as in parts of Asia, but unlike many of its major European rivals, it has so far failed to find a large international telecoms partner.
The Treasury announced in August it wanted debt-ladden IRI to float its remaining 64 percent stake in Stet by March 31, 1997.

Before the sell-off process can begin, parliament has to set up a watchdog body to cover the telecoms sector. The government hopes the necessary legislation will be ratified by Christmas, but the bill is tied to a controversial draft law on television ownership which may delay ratification.
